errors.claim: Open Kanban is positioned as the recovery of the public-domain method underneath the proprietary overlays.
errors.source_check: The source calls Open Kanban "free, open source, collaborative friendly" and criticises "proprietary ideas and interpretations"; it never calls the underlying method public-domain or describes recovery from overlays.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to Open Kanban is positioned as a free, open-source, collaborative-friendly response to proprietary ideas and interpretations of Kanban

errors.claim: Each value is given a gloss that ties it to its Lean/Agile lineage and to the pull/empowerment mechanics Kanban requires.
searches: Focus on Value|Communication and Collaboration|Holistic or Systemic
errors.source_check: Delegation, demand-pull and empowerment are attached specifically to Respect and Courage. The other values are glossed through value/waste, teamwork, and holistic system change.
errors.suggested_fix: add qualifier pull and empowerment are developed specifically under Respect and Courage

errors.claim: Value and waste-elimination are named as two sides of the same coin [V].
searches: waste|Muda|does not add value|creation of value
errors.source_check: The source says value is "frequently ... mentioned as the reverse side of the coin: eliminate waste"; the reference sentence is a paraphrase, not verbatim wording.

errors.claim: Open Kanban deliberately declines to require WIP limits, even though most contemporary Kanban frameworks do.
errors.source_check: The source says Open Kanban does not ask readers to limit WIP and instead requests batch-size reduction. It says nothing about what most contemporary frameworks require.
errors.suggested_fix: delete even though most contemporary Kanban frameworks do

errors.claim: The author frames the fourth practice as the step beyond the first three.
errors.source_check: The list contains three earlier practices, but the source itself says "The four previous practices" when introducing item 4. The reference silently resolves this internal source miscount.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to The fourth listed practice follows three prior items, although the source itself calls them "the four previous practices"

errors.claim: W. Edwards Deming, System of Profound Knowledge, is cited as theoretical grounding for the Holistic or Systemic Approach to Change value.
errors.source_check: The source says only "Deming's System of Profound Knowledge"; the forenames and initial are not present.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to Deming, System of Profound Knowledge

errors.claim: Eliyahu M. Goldratt, Theory of Constraints, is cited as theoretical grounding for the Holistic or Systemic Approach to Change value.
errors.source_check: The source says only "Goldratt's Theory of Constraints"; the forename and initial are not present.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to Goldratt, Theory of Constraints

errors.claim: Toyota Production System is cited as the Japanese origin of Kanban, where it is カンバン / Kamban.
errors.source_check: The source says the Lean movement originated in Japan and that "this type of Kanban" is called カンバン (Kamban). It links the word Japan to a Toyota Production System page but does not call TPS the origin of Kanban.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to The source links Japan to Toyota Production System, says Lean originated in Japan, and calls this type of Kanban カンバン (Kamban)

errors.claim: Free Software Foundation, four freedoms of free software, is the model for Open Kanban's four freedoms.
errors.source_check: The source names the Open Source movement and the four essential freedoms of free software and links to gnu.org; it never names the Free Software Foundation.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to the open-source movement's four essential freedoms of free software

errors.claim: David J. Anderson is the most widely-known contemporary Kanban author and the author of Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business (2010).
errors.source_check: absent; the source never names Anderson or that book, and its occurrences of 2010 are unrelated hyperlink components.

errors.claim: Most contemporary readers would understand the source's proprietary-Kanban critique as the Lean Kanban University / Anderson-tradition framing.
errors.source_check: The source criticises proprietary ideas and interpretations but names neither Lean Kanban University nor Anderson and makes no claim about readers' likely interpretation.

errors.claim: "With growth also came a push to align Kanban ... with some proprietary ideas and interpretations of what Kanban is" [V].
searches: However with growth|with growth also came|With growth also came
errors.source_check: The source begins "However with growth also came ...". The reference drops "However" and capitalises "With" without marking the alteration.
errors.suggested_fix: correct to "However with growth also came a push to align Kanban ... with some proprietary ideas and interpretations of what Kanban is"

errors.claim: The WIP position is a deliberate departure from the dominant Kanban framing.
searches: consequence|not the other way around|does not ask
errors.source_check: The source contrasts WIP limiting with batch-size reduction but never characterises another framing as dominant.
errors.suggested_fix: delete the dominant-field comparison and retain the source's explicit consequence-not-equivalence contrast

errors.claim: Continuous improvement requires a learning structure (retrospectives, strategy meetings, or Kaizen Groups) to be real.
searches: part of the culture|part of the workflow
errors.source_check: The source requires learning to become part of the culture and workflow, but says there are many implementation routes and that teams "could have" retrospectives, strategy meetings, or Kaizen Groups.
errors.suggested_fix: add qualifier retrospectives, strategy meetings, and Kaizen Groups are optional examples among many ways to implement the practice
